data.title: Guiding principle: contain the Blast Radius
bullets: Never grant agents unrestricted access to your primary machine
Assume things can go wrong: rogue commands, bugs, or unexpected behaviors
Protect against prompt injection triggered during external operations
Prevent data exfiltration and exposure of personal files or credentials
data.speaker_notes: Security is the main reason behind my setup. I don't want to give an autonomous agent full access to my main machine. You always need to contain the blast radius in case something goes wrong—whether it's a security breach, data exfiltration, or a prompt injection triggered while the agent is processing external data.

data.speaker_notes: To achieve this isolation, I run a self-hosted Hermes agent inside a local Linux virtual machine. In my specific setup, I created a Linux VM and put Docker inside it to run the agent. However, you don't necessarily need Docker: you can simply spin up a local VM—either CLI-only or with a full GUI—and run the agent directly inside it.

data.title: My setup: Segmentation over simplicity
bullets: Segment context and responsibility instead of keeping everything unified
Both for privacy reason, security and for tighter control of results
If an agent goes off the rails, the blast radius is contained within its own gateway
The conversation with my personal agents will never splill to family agent
Putting offline a system, don't stop the others
Testing cutting-edge features vs stability of workflows
data.speaker_notes: In my setup, I prefer segmenting context rather than keeping everything unified—both for privacy reasons and for greater control over the results. If an agent misbehaves, the blast radius stays contained within that specific gateway. Concretely, I have a dedicated agent for my personal productivity, one for family matters, one for each project I run (such as our ethical purchasing group or my education and technology side project), and one for each fun project, like the one dedicated to study and learning.

Tools Hermes uses to access the Internet
bullets: **web_search**: Search the web to discover relevant pages and information
**web_extract**: Extract clean, structured content from web pages
**browser_use**: Interactive browser automation (also used when `web_search` and `web_extract` are unavailable)
**`curl`**: If none of these tools are available, the agent falls back to a simple `curl`
data.speaker_notes: Hermes has three main tools that together give the agent visibility on the internet: web_search, web_extract, and browser_use. If web_search and web_extract are not available, the agent can use browser_use. And if none of these tools are available at all, the agent ultimately falls back to a simple curl command.

data.speaker_notes: When configuring browser automation in Hermes, there are two main families of browsers you can use: cloud-based browsers and local browsers. Among cloud options, you have services like Browserbase or Browser Use. Among local options, you can use Camoufox, Lightpanda, Chromium-compatible local browsers with Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), or a browser installed directly on the machine where Hermes runs.

data.title: Search with SearXNG
data.sentence: SearXNG is a metasearch engine, aggregating the results of other search engines while not storing information about its users.
bullets: Removing private data from requests going to search services
Not forwarding anything from third party services through search services (e.g. advertisement)
Removing private data from requests going to the results pages
Self-hosted on my Hermes VM via a Docker container (easy)

data.title: Extract with Firecrawl
data.sentence: Turn websites into LLM-ready markdown and structured data
bullets: Clean, LLM-ready output (Markdown, structured JSON, screenshots) that saves tokens
Makes agent-readable JS-heavy and dynamic pages
Parses web-hosted media such as PDFs and DOCX files
Self-hosted on my Hermes VM via a Docker container (medium complexity)
data.speaker_notes: Firecrawl turns complex websites into clean, LLM-ready markdown or structured JSON so agents spend fewer tokens and get higher quality context. It handles rotating proxies, JS-heavy rendering, rate limits, and even PDF/DOCX parsing automatically, and is available both as a hosted service (with 500 free credits per month) and as an open-source project.
